title: A tie-break reordered to group its parameters by kind, proved equal under the stated reordering
summary: The last-writer-wins tie-break took its two writes interleaved, `(tsA, nodeA, tsB, nodeB)`; a developer groups the parameters by kind, timestamps first, and writes the body as the comparison chain the javadoc describes. A regression proof needs the same signature in both versions, and this one changed. The developer states the relation instead, `winner(tsA, nodeA, tsB, nodeB)` from the new parameters, and the proof is of the new method against the previous one called that way, on every input.

change.description: Group the parameters by kind, `winner(tsA, tsB, nodeA, nodeB)`, so that a call reads as the two keys it compares, timestamps then node ids, and write the body as that comparison chain: `Long.compare` on the timestamps, `Integer.compare` on the node ids when they tie, the first write winning on a non-negative order. The two tests and the law in the properties file are updated to the new order.

risk: A signature change is where a regression proof usually stops: the harness calls both versions on the same arguments, and these versions do not take the same arguments. Without a proof, the rewrite rests on four test cases and a reading of `Long.compare` and `Integer.compare` against the two `if` statements they replace. A comparison chain that returned the first write on a strictly positive order, or compared the node ids in the wrong direction, would pass a test suite that never ties two writes exactly, and would make replicas that see the writes in different orders keep different values.
explanation: The developer gives the previous version's arguments as expressions over the new parameters, `tsA, nodeA, tsB, nodeB`. The tool resolves the previous version in the old classes, checks that its return type is the new one's, type-checks each expression against the parameter it is passed as (an array would be passed by name, a cast written as `(int) (end - start)`), and compiles them into the harness: the statement proved is that on every `tsA`, `tsB`, `nodeA`, `nodeB`, the new `winner(tsA, tsB, nodeA, nodeB)` returns what the old `winner(tsA, nodeA, tsB, nodeB)` returned, or throws what it threw. The comparison chain is proved equal to the two `if` statements over all 2^192 inputs in about a second; the real bytecode of `Long.compare` and `Integer.compare`, from the JDK image, is in the proof. The report names the relation in the proof line, and a counterexample would be shown as both versions received it: the new parameters, and the previous version's arguments computed from them.
resolution: Merge. The expression after `previousArguments` is what a reviewer approves: that the new parameter order maps onto the old one as stated, which is the one claim of the pull request the compiler cannot check, since every argument is a number.
notes: The library's test of the same shape (a `(long, int, long, int)` tie-break regrouped as `(long, long, int, int)` and written as a comparison chain) proves in about a second with JBMC and in 0.1 s with the tool's own checker; the measurement on this kernel is the pipeline's.

Without `previousArguments`, the tool refuses: `the previous version takes (long, int, long, int) and the new one (long, long, int, int); give the previous version's arguments as expressions over the new parameters with --before-arguments`. A method renamed or moved is named with `previousSymbol` (`--before-target`) as well.
An input for which an argument expression throws, a division by zero say, is outside the relation and skipped, as an input in the declared scope is; the expressions here cannot throw.

A rewrite that returned the first write only on a strictly positive order is found by the same proof: the library's test shows the counterexample as `winner(tsA=0, tsB=0, nodeA=0, nodeB=0), previously winner(tsA=0, nodeA=0, tsB=0, nodeB=0)`, before 0 and after 1.
provenance: Constructed on the last-writer-wins kernel of example 022, which the law in the properties file holds antisymmetric; the reordering is the one that makes the call read as the comparator it is. The technique is regression verification under a stated relation between the versions' inputs.

references.title: Shapiro, Preguiça, Baquero and Zawirski, A comprehensive study of Convergent and Commutative Replicated Data Types (LWW-Register, section 3.2.1)
Godlin and Strichman, Regression verification: proving the equivalence of similar programs (2013)
